title: On the Symbiosis of Learning and Forgetting esearchgate.net/publication/285521281_On_the_symbiosis_of_learning_remembering_and_forgetting
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 17, 2024 — original paper: https://www.r
summary: Barton summarises Robert Bjork's argument that learning and forgetting are symbiotic rather than opposed processes. Rather than treating forgetting as pure loss, Bjork shows it plays a functional role in learning by improving retrieval efficiency and reducing interference between old and new information. The piece surveys retrieval-induced forgetting, the spacing effect, the encoding variability model, and the role of context in retrieval, tying them together under the claim that forgetting is adaptive. Barton draws out the implication that students hold an inaccurate mental model of themselves as learners, often assuming exposure alone guarantees retention. He argues teachers need greater metacognitive sophistication themselves in order to design instruction — such as spaced repetition and interleaving — that deliberately uses forgetting to strengthen future learning.
points: Forgetting is reframed as functional: letting information become harder to retrieve, then retrieving it again, strengthens the memory trace more than never forgetting it at all.
Retrieval practice is positioned as essential, not optional, because the act of retrieving is itself what re-strengthens a memory.
Students commonly hold a faulty mental model of learning (exposure equals mastery); Barton argues teachers must explicitly correct this.
Teachers need stronger metacognitive awareness of their own teaching decisions to exploit the learning-forgetting relationship deliberately.
quotes: Forgetting can actually facilitate learning. When students forget something, it can make it more difficult to retrieve that information later, which in turn can make subsequent learning more effective.
Retrieval practice is essential for learning. When students retrieve information from memory, they are strengthening the memory trace and making it more likely to be recalled in the future.

Students often have faulty mental models of themselves as learners. They may believe that simply exposing themselves to information is enough to learn it, or that they will remember everything they study.
Teachers need to become more metacognitively sophisticated. This means that they need to be aware of their own learning processes and how to manage them effectively.
Teachers who understand this relationship are better equipped to create learning experiences that promote long-term retention and transfer.
